chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: The initials GPT stand for Generative Pre-trained Transformer.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: So that first word is straightforward enough, these are bots that generate new text.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Pre-trained refers to how the model went through a process of learning from a massive amount of data,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and the prefix insinuates that there's more room to fine-tune it on specific tasks with additional training.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: But the last word, that's the real key piece.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: A transformer is a specific kind of neural network, a machine learning model,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and it's the core invention underlying the current boom in AI.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: What I want to do with this video and the following chapters

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is go through a visually driven explanation for what actually happens inside a transformer.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: We're going to follow the data that flows through it and go step by step.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: There are many different kinds of models that you can build using transformers.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Some models take in audio and produce a transcript.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: This sentence comes from a model going the other way around, producing synthetic speech just from text.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: All those tools that took the world by storm in 2022, like Dolly and Midjourney,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: that take in a text description and produce an image, are based on transformers.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: And even if I can't quite get it to understand what a pie creature is supposed to be,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: I'm still blown away that this kind of thing is even remotely possible.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: And the original transformer, introduced in 2017 by Google,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: was invented for the specific use case of translating text from one language into another.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: But the variant that you and I will focus on, which is the type that underlies tools like chatGPT,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: will be a model that's trained to take in a piece of text,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: maybe even with some surrounding images or sound accompanying it,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and produce a prediction for what comes next in the passage.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: That prediction takes the form of a probability distribution

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: over many different chunks of text that might follow.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: At first glance, you might think that predicting the next word feels like a very different goal

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: from generating new text.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: But once you have a prediction model like this,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: a simple thing you could try to make it generate a longer piece of text

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is to give it an initial snippet to work with,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: have it take a random sample from the distribution it just generated,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: append that sample to the text,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and then run the whole process again to make a new prediction,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: based on all the new text, including what it just added.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: I don't know about you, but it really doesn't feel like this should actually work.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: In this animation, for example, I'm running GPT-2 on my laptop,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and having it repeatedly predict and sample the next chunk of text

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: to generate a story based on the seed text.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: And the story just doesn't actually really make that much sense.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: But if I swap it out for API calls to GPT-3 instead,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: which is the same basic model, just much bigger,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: suddenly, almost magically, we do get a sensible story,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: one that even seems to infer that a pie creature would live in a land of math and computation.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: This process here of repeated prediction and sampling

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is essentially what's happening when you interact with chat-gpt,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: or any of these other large language models,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and you see them producing one word at a time.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: In fact, one feature that I would very much enjoy

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is the ability to see the underlying distribution for each new word that it chooses.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Let's kick things off with a very high-level preview of how data flows through a transformer.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: We will spend much more time motivating and interpreting

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and expanding on the details of each step,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: but in broad strokes, when one of these chatbots generates a given word,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: here's what's going on under the hood.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: First, the input is broken up into a bunch of little pieces.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: These pieces are called tokens,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and in the case of text, these tend to be words,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: or little pieces of words, or other common character combinations.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: If images or sound are involved,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: then tokens could be little patches of that image,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: or little chunks of that sound.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Each one of these tokens is then associated with a vector,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: meaning some list of numbers,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: which is meant to somehow encode the meaning of that piece.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: If you think of these vectors as giving coordinates in some very high-dimensional space,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: words with similar meanings tend to land on vectors

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: that are close to each other in that space.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: This sequence of vectors then passes through an operation that's known as an attention block,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and this allows the vectors to talk to each other

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and pass information back and forth to update their values.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: For example, the meaning of the word model in the phrase a machine learning model

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is different from its meaning in the phrase a fashion model.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: The attention block is what's responsible for figuring out

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: which words in the context are relevant to updating the meanings of which other words,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and how exactly those meanings should be updated.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: And again, whenever I use the word meaning,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: this is somehow entirely encoded in the entries of those vectors.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: After that, these vectors pass through a different kind of operation,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and depending on the source that you're reading,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: this will be referred to as a multi-layer perceptron,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: or maybe a feed-forward layer.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: And here, the vectors don't talk to each other.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: They all go through the same operation in parallel.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: And while this block is a little bit harder to interpret,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: later on we'll talk about how the step is a little bit like asking a long list of questions

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: about each vector, and then updating them based on the answers to those questions.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: All of the operations in both of these blocks look like a giant pile of matrix multiplications,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and our primary job is going to be to understand how to read the underlying matrices.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: I'm glossing over some details about some normalization steps that happen in between,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: but this is, after all, a high-level preview.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: After that, the process essentially repeats.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: You go back and forth between attention blocks and multi-layer perceptron blocks,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: until at the very end, the hope is that all of the essential meaning of the passage

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: has somehow been baked into the very last vector in the sequence.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: We then perform a certain operation on that last vector

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: that produces a probability distribution over all possible tokens,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: all possible little chunks of text, that might come next.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: And like I said, once you have a tool that predicts what comes next given a snippet of text,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: you can feed it a little bit of seed text and have it repeatedly play this game of predicting

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: what comes next, sampling from the distribution, appending it, and then repeating over and over.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Some of you in the know may remember how, long before chat-gpt came into the scene,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: this is what early demos of gpt3 looked like.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: You would have it auto-complete stories and essays based on an initial snippet.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: To make a tool like this into a chatbot, the easiest starting point is to have a little bit

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: of text that establishes the setting of a user interacting with a helpful AI assistant,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: what you would call the system prompt, and then you would use the user's initial question,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: or prompt, as the first bit of dialogue, and then you have it start predicting

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: what such a helpful AI assistant would say in response.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: There is more to say about an added step of training that's required to make this work well,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: but at a high level, this is the general idea.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: In this chapter, you and I are going to expand on the details of what happens

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: at the very beginning of the network, at the very end of the network,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and I also want to spend a lot of time reviewing some important bits of background knowledge,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: things that would have been second nature to any machine learning engineer

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: by the time transformers came around.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: If you're comfortable with that background knowledge and a little impatient,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: you could probably feel free to skip to the next chapter,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: which is going to focus on the attention blocks,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: generally considered the heart of the transformer.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: After that, I want to talk more about these multi-layer perceptron blocks,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: how training works, and a number of other details that will have been skipped up to that point.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: For broader context, these videos are additions to a mini-series about deep learning,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and it's okay if you haven't watched the previous ones, I think you can do it out of order,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: but before diving into transformers specifically,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: I do think it's worth making sure that we're on the same page

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: about the basic premise and structure of deep learning.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: At the risk of stating the obvious, this is one approach to machine learning,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: which describes any model where you're using data to somehow determine how a model behaves.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: What I mean by that is, let's say you want a function that takes in an image,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and it produces a label describing it,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: or our example of predicting the next word given a passage of text,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: or any other task that seems to require some element of intuition and pattern recognition.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: We almost take this for granted these days, but the idea with machine learning is that

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: rather than trying to explicitly define a procedure for how to do that task in code,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: which is what people would have done in the earliest days of AI,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: instead, you set up a very flexible structure with tunable parameters,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: like a bunch of knobs and dials, and then, somehow,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: you use many examples of what the output should look like for a given input

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: to tweak and tune the values of those parameters to mimic this behavior.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: For example, maybe the simplest form of machine learning is linear regression,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: where your inputs and outputs are each single numbers,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: something like the square footage of a house and its price,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and what you want is to find a line of best fit through this data,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: you know, to predict future house prices.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: That line is described by two continuous parameters,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: say the slope and the y-intercept,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and the goal of linear regression is to determine those parameters to closely match the data.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Needless to say, deep learning models get much more complicated.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: GPT-3, for example, has not two, but 175 billion parameters.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: But here's the thing, it's not a given that you can create some giant model

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: with a huge number of parameters without it either grossly overfitting the training data,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: or being completely intractable to train.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Deep learning describes a class of models that in the last couple decades

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: have proven to scale remarkably well.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: What unifies them is that they all use the same training algorithm,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: it's called backpropagation, we talked about it in previous chapters,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and the context that I want you to have as we go in

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is that in order for this training algorithm to work well at scale,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: these models have to follow a certain specific format.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: And if you know this format going in,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: it helps to explain many of the choices for how a transformer processes language,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: which otherwise run the risk of feeling kind of arbitrary.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: First, whatever kind of model you're making,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: the input has to be formatted as an array of real numbers.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: This could simply mean a list of numbers, it could be a two-dimensional array,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: or very often you deal with higher dimensional arrays,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: where the general term used is tensor.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: You often think of that input data as being progressively transformed

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: into many distinct layers,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: where again, each layer is always structured as some kind of array of real numbers,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: until you get to a final layer which you consider the output.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: For example, the final layer in our text processing model

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is a list of numbers representing the probability distribution

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: for all possible next tokens.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: In deep learning, these model parameters are almost always referred to as weights,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and this is because a key feature of these models

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is that the only way these parameters interact with the data being processed

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is through weighted sums.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: You also sprinkle some nonlinear functions throughout,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: but they won't depend on parameters.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Typically though, instead of seeing the weighted sums

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: all naked and written out explicitly like this,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: you'll instead find them packaged together

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: as various components in a matrix vector product.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: It amounts to saying the same thing,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: if you think back to how matrix vector multiplication works,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: each component in the output looks like a weighted sum.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: It's just often conceptually cleaner for you and me to think about matrices

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: that are filled with tunable parameters

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: that transform vectors that are drawn from the data being processed.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: For example, those 175 billion weights in GPT-3

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: are organized into just under 28,000 distinct matrices.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Those matrices in turn fall into eight different categories,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and what you and I are going to do is step through each one of those categories

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: to understand what that type does.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: As we go through, I think it's kind of fun to reference the specific numbers from GPT-3

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: to count up exactly where those 175 billion come from.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Even if nowadays there are bigger and better models,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: this one has a certain charm as the first large language model

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: to really capture the world's attention outside of ML communities.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Also, practically speaking, companies tend to keep much tighter lips

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: around the specific numbers for more modern networks.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: I just want to set the scene going in that as you peek under the hood

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: to see what happens inside a tool like chat-gpt,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: almost all of the actual computation looks like matrix vector multiplication.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: There's a little bit of a risk getting lost in the sea of billions of numbers,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: but you should draw a very sharp distinction in your mind

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: between the weights of the model, which I'll always color in blue or red,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and the data being processed, which I'll always color in gray.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: The weights are the actual brains.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: They are the things learned during training, and they determine how it behaves.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: The data being processed simply encodes whatever specific input

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is fed into the model for a given run, like an example snippet of text.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: With all of that as foundation, let's dig into the first step of this text processing example,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: which is to break up the input into little chunks and turn those chunks into vectors.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: I mentioned how those chunks are called tokens, which might be pieces of words or punctuation,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: but every now and then in this chapter, and especially in the next one,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: I'd like to just pretend that it's broken more cleanly into words.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Because we humans think in words,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: this will just make it much easier to reference little examples and clarify each step.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: The model has a predefined vocabulary, some list of all possible words, say 50,000 of them,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and the first matrix that we'll encounter, known as the embedding matrix,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: has a single column for each one of these words.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: These columns are what determines what vector each word turns into in that first step.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: We label it W-E, and like all the matrices we see,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: its values begin random, but they're going to be learned based on data.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Turning words into vectors was common practice in machine learning long before transformers,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: but it's a little weird if you've never seen it before,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and it sets the foundation for everything that follows,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: so let's take a moment to get familiar with it.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: We often call this embedding a word, which invites you to think of these vectors

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: very geometrically, as points in some high dimensional space.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Visualizing a list of three numbers as coordinates for points in 3D space would be no problem,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: but word embeddings tend to be much much higher dimensional.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: In GPT-3, they have 12,288 dimensions,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and as you'll see, it matters to work in a space that has a lot of distinct directions.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: In the same way that you could take a two-dimensional slice through a 3D space,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and project all the points onto that slice,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: for the sake of animating word embeddings that a simple model is giving me,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: I'm going to do an analogous thing by choosing a three-dimensional

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: slice through this very high dimensional space,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and projecting the word vectors down onto that, and displaying the results.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: The big idea here is that as a model tweaks and tunes its weights

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: to determine how exactly words get embedded as vectors during training,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: it tends to settle on a set of embeddings where directions in the space

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: have a kind of semantic meaning.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: For the simple word-to-vector model I'm running here,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: if I run a search for all the words whose embeddings are closest to that of tower,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: you'll notice how they all seem to give very similar tower-ish vibes.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: And if you want to pull up some Python and play along at home,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: this is the specific model that I'm using to make the animations.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: It's not a transformer, but it's enough to illustrate the idea

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: that directions in the space can carry semantic meaning.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: A very classic example of this is how if you take the difference

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: between the vectors for woman and man,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: something you would visualize as a little vector in the space

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: connecting the tip of one to the tip of the other,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: it's very similar to the difference between king and queen.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: So let's say you didn't know the word for a female monarch,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: you could find it by taking king, adding this woman-man direction,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and searching for the embeddings closest to that point.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: At least, kind of.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Despite this being a classic example, for the model I'm playing with,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: the true embedding of queen is actually a little farther off than this would suggest,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: presumably because the way that queen is used in training data

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is not merely a feminine version of king.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: When I played around, family relations seemed to illustrate the idea much better.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: The point is, it looks like during training, the model found it advantageous

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: to choose embeddings such that one direction in this space encodes gender information.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Another example is that if you take the embedding of Italy,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and you subtract the embedding of Germany,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and then you add that to the embedding of Hitler,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: you get something very close to the embedding of Mussolini.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: It's as if the model learned to associate some directions with Italian-ness,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and others with WWII axis leaders.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Maybe my favorite example in this vein is how in some models,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: if you take the difference between Germany and Japan,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and you add it to sushi, you end up very close to Broadwurst.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Also, in playing this game of finding nearest neighbors,

chunks.title: Transformers

chunks.text: One bit of mathematical intuition that's helpful to have in mind,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: especially for the next chapter,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is how the dot product of two vectors

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: can be thought of as a way to measure how well they align.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Computationally, dot products involve multiplying all the corresponding components,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and then adding the results,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: which is good, since so much of our computation has to look like weighted sums.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Geometrically, the dot product is positive when vectors point in similar directions,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: it's zero if they're perpendicular,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and it's negative whenever they point in opposite directions.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: For example, let's say you were playing with this model,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and you hypothesize that the embedding of cats minus cat

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: might represent a sort of plurality direction in this space.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: To test this, I'm going to take this vector and compute its dot product

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: against the embeddings of certain singular nouns,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and compare it to the dot products with the corresponding plural nouns.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: If you play around with this, you'll notice that the plural ones

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: do indeed seem to consistently give higher values than the singular ones,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: indicating that they align more with this direction.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: It's also fun how if you take this dot product with the embeddings of the words

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: one, two, three, and so on, they give increasing values,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: so it's as if we can quantitatively measure how plural the model finds a given word.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Again, the specifics for how words get embedded is learned using data.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: This embedding matrix, whose columns tell us what happens to each word,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: is the first pile of weights in our model,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and using the GPT-3 numbers, the vocabulary size specifically is 50,257,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and again, technically this consists not of words per se, but of tokens,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and the embedding dimension is 12,288.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Multiplying those tells us this consists of about 617 million weights.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Let's go ahead and add this to a running tally,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: remembering that by the end, we should count up to 175 billion.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: In the case of transformers, you really want to think of the vectors in this embedding space

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: as not merely representing individual words.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: For one thing, they also encode information about the position of that word,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: which we'll talk about later,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: but more importantly, you should think of them as having the capacity to soak in context.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: A vector that started its life as the embedding of the word king, for example,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: might progressively get tugged and pulled by various blocks in this network,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: so that by the end, it points in a much more specific and nuanced direction

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: that somehow encodes that it was a king who lived in Scotland,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and who had achieved his post after murdering the previous king.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Describing the word in a given language is a very simple task,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: but think about your own understanding of a given word.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: The meaning of that word is clearly informed by the surroundings,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and sometimes this includes context from a long distance away.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: So in putting together a model that has the ability to predict what word comes next,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: the goal is to somehow empower it to incorporate context efficiently.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: To be clear, in that very first step, when you create the array of vectors based on the input text,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: each one of those is simply plucked out of the embedding matrix.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: So initially, each one can only encode the meaning of a single word

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: without any input from its surroundings.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: But you should think of the primary goal of this network that it flows through

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: as being to enable each one of those vectors to soak up a meaning

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: that's much more rich and specific than what mere individual words could represent.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: The network can only process a fixed number of vectors at a time,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: known as its context size.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: For GPT-3, it was trained with a context size of 2048,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: so the data flowing through the network always looks like this array of 2048 columns,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: each of which has 12,000 dimensions.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: This context size limits how much text the transformer can incorporate

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: when it's making a prediction of the next word.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: This is why long conversations with certain chatbots, like the early versions of chatGPT,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: often gave the feeling of the bot kind of losing the thread of conversation as you continued too long.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: We'll go into the details of attention in due time, but skipping ahead,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: I want to talk for a minute about what happens at the very end.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Remember, the desired output is a probability distribution

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: over all tokens that might come next.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: For example, if the very last word is professor,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and the context includes words like Harry Potter,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and immediately preceding we see least favorite teacher,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and also if you give me some leeway by letting me pretend that tokens simply look like full words,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: then a well-trained network that had built up knowledge of Harry Potter

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: would presumably assign a high number to the word Snape.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: This involves two different steps.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: The first one is to use another matrix that maps the very last vector in that context

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: to a list of 50,000 values, one for each token in the vocabulary.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Then there's a function that normalizes this into a probability distribution.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: It's called softmax, and we'll talk more about it in just a second.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: But before that, it might seem a little bit weird to only use this last embedding

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: to make a prediction, when after all, in that last step,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: there are thousands of other vectors in the layer just sitting there

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: with their own context-rich meanings.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: This has to do with the fact that in the training process,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: it turns out to be much more efficient if you use each one of those vectors in the final layer

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: There's a lot more to be said about training later on,

chunks.title: Transformers

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: This matrix is called the unembedding matrix, and we give it the label wU.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Again, like all the weight matrices we see,

chunks.text: its entries begin at random, but they are learned during the training process.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Keeping score on our total parameter count,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: this unembedding matrix has one row for each word in the vocabulary,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and each row has the same number of elements as the embedding dimension.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: It's very similar to the embedding matrix, just with the order swapped,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: so it adds another 617 million parameters to the network,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: meaning our count so far is a little over a billion,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: a small but not wholly insignificant fraction of the 175 billion that we'll end up with in total.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: As the very last mini-lesson for this chapter, I want to talk more about the softmax function,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: since it makes another appearance for us once we dive into the attention blocks.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: The idea is that if you want a sequence of numbers to act as a probability distribution,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: say a distribution over all possible next words,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: then each value has to be between 0 and 1,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and you also need all of them to add up to 1.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: However, if you're playing the deep learning game,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: where everything you do looks like matrix vector multiplication,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: the outputs you get by default don't abide by this at all.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: The values are often negative or much bigger than 1, and they almost certainly don't add up to 1.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: Softmax is the standard way to turn an arbitrary list of numbers into a valid distribution,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: in such a way that the largest values end up closest to 1,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and the smaller values end up very close to 0.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: That's all you really need to know.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: But if you're curious, the way that it works is to first raise e to the power of each of the numbers,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: which means you now have a list of positive values,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and then you can take the sum of all those positive values and divide each term by that sum,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: which normalizes it into a list that adds up to 1.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: You'll notice that if one of the numbers in the input is meaningfully bigger than the rest,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: then in the output, the corresponding term dominates the distribution,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: so if you were sampling from it, you'd almost certainly just be picking the maximizing input.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: But it's softer than just picking the max, in the sense that when other values are similarly large,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: they also get meaningful weight in the distribution,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: and everything changes continuously as you continuously vary the inputs.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: In some situations, like when chat.gpt is using this distribution to create a next word,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: there's room for a little bit of extra fun by adding a little extra spice into this function,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: with a constant t thrown into the denominator of those exponents.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: We call it the temperature, since it vaguely resembles the role of temperature in certain

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: thermodynamics equations, and the effect is that when t is larger, you give more weight to the

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: lower values, meaning the distribution is a little bit more uniform, and if t is smaller,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: then the bigger values will dominate more aggressively, where in the extreme,

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: setting t equal to 0 means all of the weight goes to that maximum value.

chunks.text: For example, I'll have gpt3 generate a story with the seed text

chunks.text: once upon a time there was a, but I'm going to use different temperatures in each case.

chunks.text: and what you get ends up being a trite derivative of Goldilocks.

chunks.title: Transformers
chunks.text: A higher temperature gives it a chance to choose less likely words, but it comes with a risk.
